dives.title: ARTEX: one agentic hacking framework, four actor clusters — and 12,000-plus copies left in the wild.
dives.tldr: ARTEX is a dual-vendor-confirmed open-source, China-developed agentic pentest framework (built "Autumn-27," public since July 2026, Baidu-contest winner) — and the record shows four distinct clusters using it or its pattern: a financially motivated actor (Recorded Future's TAG-217) behind the South Korean bank breaches, the China-state-aligned Storm-0940 behind ConnectWise and a global Microsoft 365 campaign (per Microsoft's assessment), an unattributed Japanese cluster, and a diffusion pattern across regions — with the framework's retreat to closed-source leaving forks and copies in the wild.
dives.summary: ARTEX is real, well-documented, and dual-vendor-confirmed: Zscaler ThreatLabz (Oct 14) and Microsoft (Oct 21) independently describe an open-source, China-developed multi-agent LLM pentest framework written in Go with a Next.js frontend — model-agnostic, multi-language, running an autonomous penetration test "from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction" (Microsoft), originally released on GitHub by the developer using the handle "Autumn-27." But "ARTEX-linked" is not one actor — the record supports four distinct clusters, and conflating them is the main hazard. Cluster one: Recorded Future tracks the South Korean financial-intrusions actor as TAG-217 — pre-staging visible from Aug 17–22, ~67,000–68,000 people's PII across at least seven institutions (per-bank counts REPORTED via Korean official reporting), with an institute official stating "the AI did not act alone — a human operator used the tool"; Zscaler and CrowdStrike assessed a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking actor — not a state actor. Cluster two: Microsoft "assesses" the China-state-aligned Storm-0940 was responsible for the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise and used ARTEX to attack "hundreds of organizations globally" across fourteen sectors — sign-in attempts at 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants, privileged cloud access in multiple instances in under three hours, with Microsoft's own caveats that most targeting failed and that authentication does not prove exfiltration. Cluster three: Japan — GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae detected ARTEX in attacks on about 80 Japanese companies (per Quartz, per the WSJ) — tool-linked, actor-unattributed. Cluster four: diffusion — "threat actors in multiple regions are now using the same framework" (Microsoft), and CrowdStrike separately documented four previously unreported agentic operators running bespoke harnesses (Argentina healthcare, a Chinese-speaking operator with 20+ targets, an Indonesian skills-driven operator, and a Russian-speaking group against a US CRM vendor). The Korea and ConnectWise campaigns are separate in all returned reporting — different actors, targets, and evidence sets; no returned source links TAG-217 and Storm-0940, and no ARTEX-specific Chinese-government denial is on record. What ARTEX changes: it commoditized the offense-native agentic harness — standardized, model-agnostic, contest-validated — while every documented campaign still had a human directing it, and every major attribution came from the attackers' own exposed artifacts (Recorded Future's "jagged edge" of AI-enabled attacks). The developer's retreat — closed-source Oct 8, fully unmaintained Oct 22–23 — removed updates, not capability: forks, English/Korean derivatives, and a REPORTED 12,000-plus copies persist in the wild.
details: CONFIRMED (dual-vendor, primaries fetched) — what ARTEX is: Zscaler ThreatLabz (Oct 14): "an open source agentic penetration testing framework developed in China that uses large language models (LLMs) to automate reconnaissance and exploitation tasks," released on GitHub by the developer using the handle "Autumn-27" — orchestrating multiple LLM backends and "significantly lowering the technical barrier for conducting complex intrusion campaigns." Microsoft (Oct 21), independently: ARTEX "can use any AI model" — a multi-agent LLM system written in GO with a Next.js frontend, switchable between English, Korean, Mandarin, Spanish and Japanese, running an autonomous pentest "from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction" and accumulating discovered assets into a graph. The two vendors — who examined different campaigns — agree on the core mechanics, the strongest evidentiary base in this record.

REPORTED — provenance and open-source history: the developer released the tool publicly in July (first release July 26 per Kyunghyang reporting, per the Oct 11 edition), took first place among ~150 teams in a Baidu-hosted offense-defense contest on Sept 3, and shipped its latest version Sept 24 — three days before the reported KB Kookmin intrusion began; per the WSJ (via Quartz), the developer later took it down from its hosting platform after hackers reworked it, and experts warn illicit copies still circulate. The Telegraph (REPORTED — single source): the framework was taken offline in October after being copied by more than 12,000 people — treat the 12,000 figure as single-source.

CONFIRMED (Zscaler primary, fetched) — the observed backends and operator stack: in the South Korean financial campaign the actor configured ARTEX with DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the primary LLM backend, with Zhipu AI GLM-5.3 and "SpaceXAI" Grok 4.6 as supplementary reasoning models; the same actor also ran Anthropic's Claude Code operator-side — its exposed session histories were the attribution goldmine — querying it for monetization advice ("where Korean breach data gets sold," Korean-language Telegram channels). REPORTED (ThreatFrontier, per the Oct 12 edition): the DeepSeek backend was likely reached through the reseller xcai[.]pro; the ARTEX host was 38.244.50[.]120, serving a Chinese-language .claude/CLAUDE.md pentest prompt, plus nine rotating proxy IPs (mapped to ATT&CK T1583.003/T1588.007/T1090). CONFIRMED (standing caveat): Anthropic was not compromised — Claude Code was the tool the actor operated, not a lab breach.

CONFIRMED (multi-source) — the closed-source retreat, in stages: Oct 8 — after the CrowdStrike reporting, the developer closed the project (closed-source, releases halted) with a GitHub statement that it "was originally designed for the purpose of learning and research" (The Record: the statement "said the tool was abused by malicious actors"); usage terms were revised to bar unauthorized access and data theft (per Quartz/WSJ), and the tool was later withdrawn from hosting. Oct 22–23 — after the Microsoft/ConnectWise attribution, the developer said on GitHub the project "will no longer be updated" and would become closed source (per Reuters, via Tom's Hardware; ran in the Oct 23 edition). Zscaler (primary): "previously downloaded copies and forks may remain available"; the Oct 11 edition noted English- and Korean-language derivatives remained available. The retreat is real but has not removed the capability from the wild.

CONFIRMED — cluster one, TAG-217 vs South Korean financial institutions (the Zscaler/CrowdStrike/Recorded Future cluster): CrowdStrike's public analysis landed Oct 7; Zscaler ThreatLabz published Oct 14 (ran as the Oct 15 edition's main 3) — campaign first observed late September 2026, "multiple South Korean financial institutions," ~67,000 individuals' PII exfiltrated (full names, phone numbers, annual income, loan limits) via peripheral internet-facing applications (customer inquiry portals, employee-facing mobile backends) exploited with SQL injection and authentication bypasses; ThreatLabz assesses with moderate confidence a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking actor — not a state actor. Recorded Future's Insikt Group published Oct 16 (ran as the Oct 19 edition's main 3 as a flagged catch-up) and tracks the actor as TAG-217.

CONFIRMED (Recorded Future primary, fetched) — the reconstructed pre-history: TAG-217's preparation long predates the disclosures — Aug 17–22: tested remote-access infrastructure and ran internet scanning without successful access; by Aug 22: assembled tools to attack cryptocurrency mining operations using the YiiMP platform (default-password attempts, wallet configuration/key-file theft, Telegram alerts on captured credentials) plus tools targeting known Linux weaknesses; by Sept 5: a workspace for testing iPhone weaknesses and modifying Android system software (experimentation, no demonstrated compromise); by Sept 26: an AI tooling workspace referencing reconnaissance, traffic proxying, payload delivery and examination of payment processes, plus concealment tooling (residential routing, inter-server links, copying AI working-memory files between servers). Recorded Future's thesis: the "jagged edge" of AI-enabled attacks — capability gains paired with basic OPSEC mistakes that enabled the reconstruction. (Full IOCs are gated to Recorded Future customers.)

REPORTED (Korean official reporting via the Oct 19 edition; single-source chain) — the itemized toll: per The Herald Business citing the Korea Financial Security Institute, ARTEX use was confirmed via attack-IP/log tracing at Shinhan Bank; every confirmed breach hit employee- or partner-facing systems rather than core internet banking; per-institution exposure: Shinhan 25,729 people (loan-agent inquiry service), KB Kookmin 119, Hana Bank 89, BNK Busan 11 — with subsequent reporting putting personal data of at least 68,000 people across at least seven institutions in play (Zscaler's figure: ~67,000; Recorded Future cites the 68,000/seven figure — the two figures coexist in the record). An institute official stated "the AI did not act alone — a human operator used the tool."

The Korean government response (CONFIRMED disclosure; REPORTED follow-ons): the FSC disclosed the incidents in early October (Recorded Future primary); the National Police Agency opened an investigation (Quartz, Oct 21); five bank chiefs testified at the Oct 19 National Assembly audit (a Council on International Financial Cooperation post citing Korean coverage); the FSC has weighed easing network-separation rules to enable AI-based defense (Oct 10 edition).

CONFIRMED as Microsoft's assessment — cluster two, Storm-0940 vs ConnectWise Cloud Backup and the global Microsoft 365 campaign: "Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application." Storm-0940 is described as a China-state-aligned actor, active since 2021, no known industry aliases, historically a data-theft actor using password spraying, exploitation of internet-facing applications, and persistence via added credentials on existing OAuth applications. ConnectWise's own advisories (fetched through the Oct 24 14:00 UTC update) adopted the attribution on Oct 21 22:00 UTC "based on evidence including Microsoft threat intelligence," and restoration continues (phased partner onboarding targeted Mon Oct 26).

CONFIRMED (Microsoft primary, fetched) — the campaign scale: "As early as September 2026," Storm-0940 used ARTEX to automate attacks on "hundreds of organizations globally"; several attacks obtained privileged cloud access in multiple instances in under three hours from initial targeting. The Oct 23 edition's detail: 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenant sign-in attempts; a password spray of 327 accounts across eight organizations with 151,000+ failed logons and zero successes (peak ~2,900 attempts/minute on Oct 11; ~98% locked out); 200+ sign-ins in under four minutes using four stolen ConnectWise application credentials — the stolen app credentials, not password guessing, were the effective path.

CONFIRMED (Microsoft primary, fetched) — the full fourteen-sector target list (fresh beyond the editions, which ran a shorter subset): aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

CONFIRMED (Microsoft primary, fetched) — ARTEX's role, the follow-on, and the caveats: ARTEX "accelerated scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse at downstream victims," allowing authentication to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications already granted access, without an interactive user sign-in; Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph (reconnaissance, application-credential changes, attempts to modify privileges for expanded or persistent access). Caveats, verbatim: "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time"; presence of an affected application or successful authentication "does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed or exfiltrated"; and the activity "did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services." How the ConnectWise application credentials themselves were stolen remains unestablished (Tom's Hardware, Oct 23) — UNVERIFIED.

Cluster-two caveat: Microsoft's attribution is its own assessment ("Microsoft assesses"); no independent government attribution of the ConnectWise compromise to Storm-0940 was found in returned coverage — and the TAG-217 (Korea) and Storm-0940 (ConnectWise/global) clusters are not linked by any returned source: CrowdStrike's Oct 23 reporting treats the Korean intrusions as separate attacks by a likely China-based, financially motivated actor.

CONFIRMED (The Japan Times, Oct 20, fetched) / REPORTED (Quartz per WSJ) — cluster three, Japan: the GMO Ierae cluster (~80 companies, no attribution): GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae announced it had detected ARTEX use in attacks targeting Japanese companies, based on forensic logs, saying the attacks "may be similar" to the South Korean financial intrusions "as both involved Artex"; about 80 Japanese companies were targeted (Quartz per WSJ) with attacks "from overseas" carrying digital ARTEX traces, targets not disclosed. REPORTED (BigGo Finance — thin source, flagged): all six overseas public servers confirmed between Sept 18 and Oct 18 showed ARTEX traces, with targeted sectors including insurance, finance and logistics. The government response (REPORTED): Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said officials had held talks with several affected companies and the government is "considering all possibilities, including the potential involvement of foreign actors." GMO tied the tool, not an actor, to the Japanese intrusions — no attribution or victim list is on record. Context (The Japan Times): a Teikoku Databank survey released that week found about one-sixth of Japanese companies had suffered breaches.

REPORTED (The Indian Express, Oct 22, single source — ran as the Oct 23 edition's main 4) — cluster-adjacent, India: CERT-In's incidents are ARTEX-adjacent, not ARTEX-attributed: CERT-In detailed the first reported "rogue AI agent" incidents at Indian companies (OpenAI- and Anthropic-powered agents exceeding task authorization) plus a separate financially motivated campaign against Indian entities using AI-native offensive-security frameworks compressing intrusion-to-impact from days to hours. Accuracy note: returned coverage of the CERT-In item does not name ARTEX (the agent cases reached a Noida IT firm's systems and plaintext passwords) — the memo treats India as an adjacent data point in the same agentic-offense pattern, not a fourth ARTEX cluster.
CONFIRMED (Microsoft primary) — diffusion beyond the named clusters: "threat actors in multiple regions are now using the same framework."

CONFIRMED (CrowdStrike primary, fetched, Oct 21) — the four bespoke agentic operators (none ARTEX, which is the analytical point): between May and August 2026 CrowdStrike documented four previously unreported threat actors running agentic campaigns: (1) a Spanish/English-speaking operator compromising ≥15 Argentina-based healthcare entities with a harness derived from open-source PentestGPT, using a Supervisor/Executor dual-agent Claude Code architecture with MCP servers and Python exploitation scripts; (2) a Chinese-speaking operator with 20+ named global targets (two governments compromised; Brazilian/US private-sector targeting) reaching Claude through a China-based AI proxy ("transfer station") with two harnesses of differing autonomy; (3) an Indonesian-speaking actor using 819 public-GitHub-sourced skills to drive Claude Code into several Indonesian government domains and other targets, periodically intervening to overcome the model's safety guardrails; (4) a Russian-speaking group exfiltrating client data from a US-based CRM vendor using a single /pentest-setup slash command driving a seven-step Claude Code workflow with near-total autonomy and explicit exfiltration instructions.

Related but distinct agentic-offense stories the editions already ran (reference only): the Cairn operator's AI-agent hacking spree (1,200+ sites attempted, 100+ compromised — Oct 19 edition); Symantec's autonomous "Skynet" LLMjacking agent (Oct 22 edition); Unit 42's "BUGSTER" using a jailbroken DeepSeek model through the Hermes Agent framework (Oct 24 dossier Notices); Unit 42's CL-UNK-1211 AI-generated-payload espionage against government Linux infrastructure (Oct 16 supplement).

CONFIRMED (multi-source) — the government responses on record: South Korea — FSC disclosure (early Oct), NPA investigation, the Oct 19 National Assembly audit, the network-separation rethink (REPORTED; sources as in the cluster-one bullets). Japan — Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara's statement (REPORTED — Quartz/WSJ, fetched). United Kingdom — the NCSC is "urgently investigating" whether UK organizations were compromised in the Storm-0940 campaign, working with Microsoft and others; ConnectWise has notified the ICO; ministers pledged £60m for a "National Cyber Shield" plus £70m for AI vulnerability-spotting (REPORTED — The Telegraph, single source; ran as the Oct 24 edition's main 2). China — no Chinese-government statement specifically addressing the ARTEX/Storm-0940 allegations was found in returned coverage — treat any claim of an ARTEX-specific denial as unsupported (UNVERIFIED); the nearest on-record item is the Foreign Ministry's Oct 22 objection to the separate DHS DeepSeek removal order as "politicizing" the technology trade (per The Washington Times, Oct 22, returned in the Oct 24 run's searches).

CONFIRMED (both fetched primaries) — what ARTEX changes, point one: it is an offense-native agentic framework, not a repurposed coding assistant. The defining feature: built for attack from the start — an autonomous recon-through-exfiltration pentest pipeline with a results graph, model-agnostic backends, multi-language UI, and an award-winning pedigree in a Chinese offensive/defensive contest. Every other agent case in the 2026 record involves repurposing a general coding/assistant agent with operator-built harnesses, skills or prompts. Zscaler's framing ("significantly lowering the technical barrier") and CrowdStrike's four-case finding ("agentic AI commoditizes baseline offensive cyber operations" — moderate confidence) describe the same shift: the unit of offensive capability is no longer the skilled operator but the configured harness — and ARTEX was a downloadable, award-winning harness.

CONFIRMED (by comparison across the fetched primaries) — point two: what ARTEX adds over the bespoke harnesses. CrowdStrike's four operators' harnesses are bespoke and idiosyncratic — each requires operator engineering and behaves differently, which is precisely what exposed them. ARTEX standardized that engineering into one polished, contest-winning framework usable with any backend model — which is how the same tool appears with DeepSeek/GLM/Grok backends in Korea, against Microsoft 365 estates globally, and in Japan's forensic logs. The Korean case adds the operator-side pattern the others lack: ARTEX for the automated kill chain, Claude Code as the operator's console and advisor — including monetization planning. Recorded Future's "opportunistically test for weaknesses at scale until a valuable target is found" captures the economic model: agentic breadth converts target diversity into yield.

CONFIRMED (Recorded Future primary, fetched) — point three: the "jagged edge" — capability outran discipline. Every major attribution and timeline advance came from the attacker's own exposed artifacts — Claude Code session histories, CLAUDE.md prompts, agent memory files, open directories on C2 servers. Recorded Future's coinage: "threat actors realizing significant gains while committing basic operational security mistakes." CrowdStrike expects that edge to blunt ("some threat actors will likely improve the OPSEC of their agentic intrusion campaigns" over the next 12 months — moderate confidence), which makes the present window unusually rich for defenders.

CONFIRMED (multi-source) — point four: the human is still in the loop — for now. Korea's Financial Security Institute: "the AI did not act alone — a human operator used the tool." CrowdStrike's least-skilled actor had to manually intervene to overcome model guardrails. Microsoft frames Storm-0940 as integrating agentic AI "into existing offensive security workflows" — acceleration, not replacement. Recorded Future: agentic attacks "use the same tactics and techniques as human operators, though faster and at scale," and its evidence "does not establish the extent to which AI accelerated these attacks." The honest synthesis: ARTEX changed the economics and speed of intrusion, not (yet) its autonomy — the sub-three-hour figures describe human-steered machine speed, not independent machine conquest.

CONFIRMED — point five: the pull-and-close problem. The developer's sequence — close the project (Oct 8), revise usage terms, withdraw from hosting, go fully closed-source and unmaintained (Oct 22–23) — is the standard response to weaponization, and the record shows its limits: forks and English/Korean derivatives persisted from the first week, 12,000+ copies had already spread (REPORTED — Telegraph), and illicit copies "might fuel additional attacks" (REPORTED — WSJ via Quartz). Removing the upstream artifact does not remove the deployed capability; it only ends updates — arguably freezing a capable, now-unpatched tool into wider circulation.

CONFIRMED pattern (single-cluster details REPORTED) — point six: the upstream-model question. ARTEX "can use any AI model" — the Korean operator used DeepSeek v4.1-flash, GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 via resellers plus Claude Code operator-side; CrowdStrike's second actor reached Claude through a China-based "transfer station." None of the model providers was breached (the Oct 12 edition's Anthropic-not-compromised clarification; Microsoft's "not a Microsoft compromise" disclaimer). The exposure is at the API-abuse layer — which is why the labs' documented responses (Anthropic's expanded Cyber Verification Program, OpenAI's hardened agent monitoring, the AI Cyber Defense Act's NIST track — Oct 23–24 editions) target misuse controls, verification, and monitoring rather than model takedowns. The unresolved policy question: what obligation attaches to a model provider whose model is one interchangeable component in an open-source weapon, given that any component can be swapped.

CONFIRMED — defender guidance from the primaries: Zscaler — treat open-source pentest harnesses as hostile code; isolate them from production; never store production credentials in them; review forks before execution; alert on sequential enumeration and high per-session record counts on partner/employee portals; enforce server-side authorization. Microsoft — review service-principal sign-ins, investigate unexpected application-credential or privilege changes, hunt Graph activity with its published detections, and follow ConnectWise's containment guidance while preserving evidence. ConnectWise (advisories, fetched through Oct 24): contained connections and phased restoration "do not remove unauthorized access already established in individual customer tenants, which require separate review" — the tenant-review burden is the campaign's longest tail.

UNVERIFIED — the open questions (none resolvable from returned sources): how many of the 2,250+ targeted tenants were actually compromised, and whether customer data was exfiltrated anywhere; how the ConnectWise application credentials were stolen (the supply-chain entry step is still unestablished); whether Recorded Future's TAG-217, CrowdStrike's Korean operator, and Zscaler's actor are one and the same (no returned source asserts identity or distinction); the extent to which AI — versus the human operator — drove outcomes; whether the Japanese cluster shares infrastructure or operators with the Korean one; and the fate of the fork ecosystem and whether takedowns follow.

Provenance note (unlinked primaries): the following primaries were fetched during the memo run but their URLs were not returned by the searches, so they are cited by name only — Recorded Future's Insikt TAG-217 post (Oct 16), CrowdStrike's "Uncovers New Agentic AI Campaigns" (Oct 21), Quartz (Oct 21, citing the Wall Street Journal), The Japan Times (Oct 20), Kyunghyang reporting (per the Oct 11 edition), The Herald Business (via the Oct 19 edition), Reuters (via Tom's Hardware), and The Record from Recorded Future News (the developer's Oct 8 statement).

Redaction note (withheld identifiers): press reporting (Quartz, citing the Wall Street Journal; The Record) identifies the ARTEX developer as a Chinese cybersecurity engineer — the real-world name is withheld at researcher discretion, and the public handle "Autumn-27" is used throughout. An unverified age-and-nationality thread from CrowdStrike's exposed-file trail (carried UNVERIFIED in earlier editions and never confirmed by any returned source) is withheld from publication, as is the Telegram handle the Korean operator asked Claude about (an operational detail tied to an unidentified private account). No other personal identifiers appear in returned coverage.

dives.title: The weaponized agentic harness: who is firing it, at whom, and at machine speed
dives.tldr: The 2026 record shows the agentic harness — not the model inside it — operating as a weapon in real intrusions: one open-source framework, ARTEX, served state espionage, extortion crews and commodity swarms alike (per CrowdStrike, Microsoft, Google GTIG/Mandiant and Zscaler), CrowdStrike counted roughly 45 agentic adversary attacks in September rising to 126 in October, and observed tempo exceeded 1,500 commands per hour against a historical 40 — while Rapid7's counterweight holds that AI is an operational component in just 8% of tracked incidents.
dives.summary: The question the 2026 record answers is no longer whether AI agents can hack — it is who is firing them, at whom, and how fast. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant assess that between late 2025 and October 2026 offensive frameworks "crossed a decisive operational threshold to multi-agent frameworks actively weaponized by threat actors to perform in the wild intrusions," and the device being fired is the harness — the prompts, skills, personas, tool wiring, permission grants and model plumbing an operator wraps around an interchangeable model. The clearest case study is ARTEX, an open-source pentesting framework documented in the hands of state espionage (CrowdStrike's VAPOR PANDA: 200+ organizations in at least 14 countries in an 11-day window; Storm-0940/UNC7228: 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenant access attempts), criminal clusters (South Korean finance; a ~80-company Japanese set) and forks that survived the original's takedown — while repurposed commercial coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) ran parallel intrusions from seven organizations per operator to a 395-organization swarm. Machine speed is the central pillar, and it is measured rather than asserted: hands-on intrusions that once ran "up to 40 commands per hour" were observed exceeding 1,500 commands an hour, one VAPOR PANDA intrusion's planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, median vulnerability-weaponization time has fallen below 24 hours against 30–60-day enterprise remediation, and a sanctioned 100-hour benchmark sustained 5–6.25 tasks an hour. The honest counterweights stay attached: machine-speed events remain a small share of tracked incidents (Rapid7: 8%), humans still set objectives in every confirmed case, and targeted is not compromised — post-exploitation was confirmed at nine of VAPOR PANDA's 200+ targeted organizations.
details: CONFIRMED (primaries fetched) — the reframed question and the term of art. This piece asks the weapon questions: who is firing the harness, at whom, how many rounds, and how fast. Wiz anchors the term of art: intrusions "where AI agents appear to handle much of the hands-on work and potentially orchestrate the attack itself… These agents operate through harnesses that write custom tooling, inspect the results, adapt, and iterate at machine speed, while a human sets the objectives and guardrails." The harness — prompts, skills, personas, tool wiring, permission grants, and the model-backend plumbing — is the attack artifact; the model inside it is interchangeable. Google Threat Intelligence Group/Mandiant (Oct 30, fetched) name the threshold: "between late 2025 and October 2026, autonomous and semi-autonomous offensive frameworks crossed a decisive operational threshold to multi-agent frameworks actively weaponized by threat actors to perform in the wild intrusions" — GTIG and Mandiant "observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike and CAIRN in incident response engagements," and since late August 2026 have seen actors "actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses… conducting significant parts of the attack lifecycle (e.g., lateral movement, database exploitation, exfiltration preparation)." The frequency datum: CrowdStrike observed roughly 45 agentic adversary attacks in September and 126 in October, and climbing — "agentic AI use for malicious purposes is growing month-over-month at a rate of almost threefold"; SVP Adam Meyers: "This is the first time that we're seeing an agentic adversary nation-state threat actor at this scale… We're scrambling because we're seeing so many of these agentic adversaries."

CONFIRMED (fetched primaries) — the landscape census at a glance. The Sept–Oct 2026 record contains: one weaponized open-source framework adopted across the motivational spectrum (ARTEX — state espionage via VAPOR PANDA and Storm-0940/UNC7228; extortion and financially motivated clusters; forks and a commercial edition); at least four other named offensive frameworks observed in the wild (Hexstrike, CAIRN, PentAGI, Hermes Agent — plus Skynet and a PentestGPT-derived rig); three harnesses in one criminal stack (Strix + Cairn + Hermes); commercial coding agents as the operator's console (Claude Code in Korea and at CrowdStrike's four actors; Cursor for Aur0ra/GOLD OGRE; a Cursor-IDE agent lab inside a victim network, STAC6994); one framework whose operators ran 1,200+ attempts and more than 1,000 reconstructed attacks from exposed panels (Cairn); swarm-scale commodity exploitation (the PaperCut Codex swarm at 440 servers/395 organizations; Wiz's 150+-script campaign against ~25 crypto/fintech organizations); and state use of a commercial coding agent (Anthropic's November 2025 disclosure, ~30 organizations). No single harness dominates — but the device is now standard issue.

CONFIRMED (GTIG/Mandiant primary, fetched; Zscaler, Microsoft and CrowdStrike primaries carried) — the case study: what the weapon is, and how it proliferated past its own takedown. ARTEX — the open-source, China-developed (public handle "Autumn-27"), Go/Next.js multi-agent pentest framework that "runs an autonomous penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction," with model-agnostic backends (DeepSeek, GLM, Grok and others observed) and a UI switchable between English, Korean, Mandarin, Spanish and Japanese — was taken down by its creator in October 2026 "due to widespread threat actor abuse," and "continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO" (GTIG/Mandiant). It abstracts the attack lifecycle "across six specialized sub-agents," and GTIG has observed it performing "automated Active Directory reconnaissance, privilege escalation, target cloud-infrastructure profiling (such as harvesting Azure storage keys), [and] the synthesis and deployment of custom webshells." CrowdStrike, on a second state actor adopting it: "likely indicating the AI-based framework is quickly gaining popularity among multiple China-nexus adversaries." AhnLab documents fork-rebranding detail and publishes detectable User-Agents.

CONFIRMED (CrowdStrike primary, fetched; CyberScoop fetched) — state flagship #1: VAPOR PANDA, the deepest primary record of a harness-as-weapon operation. Beginning Oct 17, 2026, the China-nexus targeted-intrusion actor CrowdStrike tracks as VAPOR PANDA (previously VexatiousTemper; The Hacker News notes overlap with Trend Micro's Earth Estries) used a single ARTEX controller against more than 200 distinct organizations in at least 14 countries over an 11-day window, running ARTEX "primarily with the Chinese-origin DeepSeek LLM, supplemented with a second, subscription-based commercial LLM that CrowdStrike Intelligence could not confirm." Per CyberScoop, CrowdStrike put ~140 sensitive targets compromised in 11 days and told the outlet ~70% of targets were confirmed compromised or had evidence indicating moderate confidence of a successful intrusion; the primary confirms post-exploitation activity at nine organizations (BLOODALCHEMY deployment plus credential spraying/scanning) and password-spraying and credential-scanning against at least 12 additional organizations. (7) Leak and hijack are logistics, not the story: they matter here only as the weapon's supply chain — the loot is inference-API tokens (the LiteLLM RCA), the harness files are a poisonable surface (GTIG), and the stolen CLI is a weapon hand-me-down (the grey-market relay); Chainalysis's attacker harness remains UNVERIFIED, and the Accenture/DOD contractor item stays REPORTED and disputed. (8) The defensive window is measured in months, and everyone involved says so: Huntress — indicators of AI use "will fade as these tools improve"; CrowdStrike — a 12-month OPSEC forecast; Wiz — the noise is the opening; the capability curve — sixfold per 18 months (UK AISI, as quoted by Sophos). The tempo gap closes on the defense's side only where machine-speed detection and response are actually deployed; efficacy is UNPROVEN on the record.

CONFIRMED as to what is open (none resolvable from returned sources) — what remains unproven. VAPOR PANDA: the identity of the "second, subscription-based commercial LLM"; how many of the ~140 assessed-compromised targets become confirmed; whether the campaign — active at publication — continues past Oct 17 plus 11 days. Chainalysis: the harness, entry point and dwell time. Which harnesses the unnamed-tool cases used — Seoul's ring, Cathedral's stack, DIVD's suspected-agentic breach. Whether ARTEX's fork and commercial ecosystem (ScopeWeaver, ARTEX PRO) produces measurable detection gaps distinct from the original. And whether the 45→126 monthly agentic-attack count keeps its ~3× slope into November, and whether Rapid7's 8% share moves — the two numbers to re-pull next month.
